clue.text: Profit-sheet he adjusted after discounting electronics – bargains can be found here

indicators.note: discounting something means leaving it out of the total, so those letters are dropped
something adjusted has been rearranged, so the remaining letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen
E is the abbreviation for electronic; the plural takes every E out

explanation.surface: An accountant reworks a profit sheet once the electronics department's figures are left out.
explanation.walkthrough: All three Es leave PROFITSHEETHE, and the ten letters left are rearranged into THRIFT SHOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A charity store selling second-hand goods cheaply is a place where people go looking for bargains.

clue.text: Post office rejected a large gemstone ...

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for Post Office
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A post office refuses to handle a big precious stone.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is an iridescent precious stone, so it is one example of a gemstone used in jewellery.

clue.text: ... or tasty apple

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold, so it describes something golden
synonym: good to eat

explanation.surface: Read on from the clue before: a large gem, or else a tasty apple.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots tie this to 2 Down, so 'or' reads as a plain conjunction; it is really the heraldic term for gold, giving GOLDEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Golden Delicious is a widely grown yellow-skinned variety of eating apple.

clue.text: Almost mount deer

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to mount a play is to stage it

explanation.surface: Climbing almost onto the back of a deer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' suggests getting on an animal, but here it is the theatrical verb, stage, which loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag is an adult male deer, so the word names one particular kind of that animal.

clue.text: Friends maybe setting my code incorrectly

indicators.note: written incorrectly, the letters come out in the wrong order and must be rearranged

blocks.note: a setting is a situation or set of circumstances
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pals setting up a coding system for each other and getting it wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Friends is the American sitcom about six New Yorkers; 'maybe' marks it as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The television show Friends is a well-known example of a sitcom, a comic series built around recurring characters.

clue.text: Funny scene in small outfit

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
kit is a set of clothes, an outfit

explanation.surface: A comic sketch performed in a tiny costume.
explanation.definitionFit: A skit is a short comic sketch, a brief humorous piece of performance.

clue.text: After being connected – oddly disappearing

indicators.note: if the odd-numbered letters vanish, only the even-placed ones are left

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Something vanishes erratically once a link has been made.
explanation.definitionFit: As a conjunction it means as soon as or when, so a sentence like 'once you arrive' equals 'after you arrive'.

clue.text: Supply hot kettle chips around noon – now things are getting interesting

indicators.note: read as the adverb from supple, meaning flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order
the shuffled letters sit around the outside of the next item

blocks.note: taken as written
N is short for noon

explanation.surface: Selling crisps cooked in a kettle at lunchtime turns out to be an exciting business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like the verb to provide, but it is supple turned into an adverb: flexibly. Kettle chips are a brand of crisps.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when a story or situation takes a turn and becomes more complicated or intriguing.

clue.text: Papers and student journalist did nothing

blocks.note: identity papers are your ID
L is a learner, as on a learner driver's plate
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A newspaper and a trainee reporter spent the day slacking.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle is to pass time without working, so the past tense means sat around being inactive.

clue.text: Pinched Grant's glove

blocks.note: a pinched face is thin and drawn
to grant permission is to let

explanation.surface: Someone has stolen a glove belonging to a person called Grant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' reads as stole and 'Grant' as a name; they are an adjective for a haggard look and the verb to allow.
explanation.definitionFit: A gauntlet is a strong glove with a long flared cuff, as worn with armour or for riding.

clue.text: Wreath that is left on the counter

indicators.note: counter means running against, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is
L is short for left

explanation.surface: A garland of flowers someone has left lying on the shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter' suggests a shop surface but means contrary, sending the letters upwards in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers worn around the neck, which is a kind of wreath.

clue.text: First episode has pace

indicators.note: the phrase before it has, that is holds, the letters inside it

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: The opening instalment of a series moves along quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in plain view across the two words before 'has', which reads as owning but means containing.
explanation.definitionFit: A step is a single stride, and a pace is likewise the length of one stride in walking.

clue.text: Old Iranian standard is raised

indicators.note: in a down answer, something raised is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: par is the normal or standard level
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ancient Persian banner is hoisted high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' suggests a flag being raised, but it means the norm, par; only 'is' goes up.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsi was the Persian of old Iran, and the word also names Zoroastrians descended from ancient Persians.

clue.text: Part of workforce in evening dress

blocks.note: evening as night-time
a shift is a simple straight-cut dress

explanation.surface: Some staff turn up for work wearing evening gowns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evening dress' reads as one formal outfit; split it, and a shift is a loose straight dress.
explanation.definitionFit: The night shift is the group of employees working overnight hours, one portion of a company's staff.

clue.text: Finally melt butter on the outside as suggested

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the next word
the second item is placed around the first, wrapping it on the outside

blocks.note: its last letter
a butter is something that butts, such as a goat

explanation.surface: Kitchen advice: melt the butter around the outside, as the recipe proposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' is the dairy spread on the surface, but it is one who butts: a goat.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting at something means hinting or implying it, so the past form fits proposed or implied.

clue.text: Egg supplier fencing in a very safe place

indicators.note: fencing in an area means enclosing it, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: a hen lays eggs
taken as written
V is short for very

explanation.surface: A poultry farmer fences in a secure spot for the birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A haven is a refuge or sanctuary where one is protected from danger.

clue.text: Give warning as climbing up red ash carelessly splits bark

indicators.note: done carelessly, the letters land in a jumbled order
in a down answer, climbing up means reading from bottom to top
to split something is to break into it, so the jumble goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a dog's bark

explanation.surface: A climber scrambling up a red ash tree splits its bark, a sign of trouble ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bark' looks like tree bark beside the ash, but it is a dog's woof, written upwards and split open.
explanation.definitionFit: To foreshadow is to hint at or signal a future event beforehand, a form of advance warning.

clue.text: US President's in that woman's bed over and over again

blocks.note: possessive pronoun for a woman
a berth is a bunk on a ship or train
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
the word once more, taken as written

explanation.surface: A scandalous tale of a president found repeatedly in a woman's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls, recorded as O on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert Hoover served as the thirty-first President of the United States, from 1929 to 1933.

clue.text: Curry for one after work, putting no-frills rice on first and expecting good stuff

indicators.note: after sends the actor's name to follow the piece for work
without its frills the word loses its edges, leaving only the inner letters
placed on the ordinal means coming right after it in an across answer

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
Tim Curry the actor is one example of a Tim
1st with the digit written as I
its inner two letters

explanation.surface: Ordering a curry after work with plain rice, hoping for a tasty meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curry' wants to be the takeaway dish; it is the actor Tim Curry, famous from The Rocky Horror Picture Show.
explanation.definitionFit: An optimistic person is hopeful and confident that things will turn out well.

clue.text: Advice: put mine back

indicators.note: put back here means read in the backward direction

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: A recommendation to return something belonging to me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like the possessive pronoun, but it is a colliery.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is a helpful hint or piece of practical guidance, the same thing as a piece of advice.

clue.text: Realises in audition for feature

indicators.note: an audition is a hearing, so the word is judged by how it is heard

blocks.note: to realise something is to know it

explanation.surface: An actor at a casting realises they have a part in a feature film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature' suggests a feature film in the audition setting; it is a facial feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial features include the eyes, mouth and nose, so the nose is one example of a feature.

clue.text: Extent of calcium deficiency not universal

indicators.note: not marks what follows as something to be taken away from the word before

blocks.note: Ca is the chemical symbol for calcium
a paucity is a shortage or lack
U is the film-certificate rating for universal

explanation.surface: A doctor gauges how far a patient's calcium shortage has spread.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film rating meaning suitable for all.
explanation.definitionFit: Capacity is the maximum amount something can hold or do, its full scope or extent.

clue.text: Fine following morning on the rampage

indicators.note: following means this piece comes after the next one in order

blocks.note: a.m. marks the morning hours
okay, all right

explanation.surface: All was well until the morning, when things went wild.
explanation.definitionFit: Running amok means behaving in a wild, uncontrolled and destructive way, like someone rampaging.

clue.text: High-pitch results when key fob is out of bounds

indicators.note: with its bounds taken out the word loses both outer letters, keeping the core

blocks.note: the Alt key on a computer keyboard
its central letter

explanation.surface: An alarm sounds when a car key fob strays too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key fob' reads as one object; the key is a keyboard key, and the fob only supplies its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Alto is the high vocal range of a countertenor or the lowest female voice, a high-pitched singing part.

clue.text: Perhaps 2001: A Space Odyssey ultimately used up Kubrick's focus

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so each word gives its final letter
in a down answer, up means read from bottom to top
the focus is the centre, so only the middle letter of the name counts

blocks.note: the last letter of each word
the fourth of its seven letters

explanation.surface: Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey consumed all his concentration.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title makes '2001' look like part of the wordplay, but it is the definition: a year.
explanation.definitionFit: The number 2001 names a particular calendar period of twelve months, so it is one example of a year.

clue.text: Second tea or coffee?

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
cha (or char) is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A host offering a second cup: tea or coffee?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a second cup, but it means a short moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a fine type of coffee, originally shipped from the Yemeni port, and also a chocolate-flavoured coffee drink.

clue.text: Quickly learn stuff

blocks.note: first meaning: to study intensively just before an exam
second meaning: to pack something tightly full

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like learning material fast; the phrase splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both last-minute revision for a test and packing a space tightly to bursting.

clue.text: Department store keep Gary Oldman's line out when broadcast

indicators.note: out means the item named just before is removed from the word
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: a keep is a castle stronghold
Gary Numan, the electronic pop singer
taken as written, without the apostrophe
L is short for line

explanation.surface: A shop insists an actor's dialogue be cut from its broadcast advert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gary Oldman' reads as the actor's full name; split it, Gary is singer Gary Numan, and Oldman loses its L before being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortnum and Mason is the famous upmarket Piccadilly store, best known for its food halls and hampers.
